subsubtopic: STRIKE BY RAILWAY WORKERS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a work stoppage by 200 rail workers in British Columbia is causing havoc with shipments of western grain. In Alberta there are 1,500 fully loaded railway cars sitting on sidings, some trains being a mile long, which cannot proceed to their destinations because of the tie-up. Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier of quality grain is being jeopardized.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave):
That the minister responsible for transport and the Wheat Board intervene personally to get this dispute settled and get western grain moving again to the markets of the world.

NECESSITY FOR PRICING AGREEMENT WITH WESTERN PROVINCES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43, Madam Speaker. Given the fact that oil production cutbacks in western Canada, and more particularly in the Weyburn area by PanCanadian, an operator of the units of 65 companies, last week resulted in the cutback of 75 per cent of their production from some 480 producing wells for which they receive $17.75 a barrel at the wellhead while the government continues to pay $40 a barrel for offshore oil, and given the fact that the gasoline price at the gasoline pumps has increased in the last year by 50 cents a gallon, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko):
That the Minister of Energy bring an end to the cold war between the east and the west which he has created and address the very serious situation, which is his responsibility, of a pricing agreement with the provinces of western Canada, which will allow western Canada to make its contribution to the energy of this great nation.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of some urgency. Statistics Canada has reported that the tourist deficit in this country for the first three months of this year was almost $1 billion, which was almost the same figure as for the same quarter of last year. In light of the potential of the tourist industry to assist in generating extra income for all sectors of the economy, and because in addition to ignoring this potential the government has placed the entire industry in jeopardy as a result of high interest rates, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz):
That the government cease its imitation of the Peace Tower clock and start working again to get the mechanism of the economy moving forward.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED TRIBUTE TO BUILDER OF WELLAND CANAL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a motion which I am sure will receive the unanimous consent of the House. Last century there was a man who had a dream and who had the courage and determination to bring that dream to life. The man was William Hamilton Merritt, and his dream was the Welland ship canal, which is now an integral part of the St. Lawrence Seaway. In order to honour the memory of the man who brought the Welland Canal into being, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That this House agree that consideration should be given by the Canadian Coast Guard to naming a vessel The William Hamilton Merritt.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Some years ago the government encouraged home ownership through the AHOP program. Today, because of its calamitous interest rate policy, the same government is threatening to deprive hundreds of their homes due to the necessity of remortgaging at 18 per cent, 19 per cent and more. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis):
That the government institute a six-month freeze on remortgaging in cases where the new interest rates will consume in excess of 30 per cent of the family income for house payments and, failing that, the government extend the subsidy, without ceiling, to the same hardship group.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Despite the fact that our small business community makes a tremendous contribution to the economic well-being of the country, is our number one creator of new and productive jobs, and is innovative and counterinflationary, the Liberal government has refused to recognize the devastating effects its misguided budgetary policies and high interests are having on this vital sector and, in turn, on the country as a whole. Because of the fact that our party can be singularly credited for forcing into effect those assistance programs which do exist, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, who obviously does not have the attention of his senior colleagues in the cabinet, cross the floor of this House and join the ranks of the Progressive Conservative party where he will be able more effectively to exercise his responsibilities.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas pensioners are among those who suffer most from the impact of high inflation which, under this government's management, has reached the ridiculous rate of 13 per cent, and whereas the government's policy of indexing the Canada Pension Plan on a yearly basis causes a loss to pensioners, due to inflation, of over 6 per cent of their yearly pensions, or about one month's rent every year-a loss they can ill afford-I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the government immediately institute a policy of indexing the CPP on a quarterly basis to ensure that Canadian pensioners do not suffer needlessly because of the government's mismanagement of the economy.

subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF URANIUM MARKETING INQUIRY FINDINGS
speechtext:
In the absence of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I would like to put my question to the Prime Minister who confirmed yesterday that the inquiry into the uranium cartel is now complete.
Oral Questions
As the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs stated on March 4 in this House that when the inquiry was completed the director's findings would be made public, and as in 1977, when the inquiry was commissioned, the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs also said that the findings of the inquiry would be made public, would the Prime Minister now inform us when he intends to make these findings public?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF URANIUM MARKETING INQUIRY FINDINGS
speechtext: Well, it would not be for me to set the date, Madam Speaker. If the minister gave that undertaking I will consult with him and see what his intentions are. The competition bureau, as I said yesterday, has referred the matter to the attorney general, and of course if he decides to lay charges the whole matter will become public in court.

subtopic: IMPACT OF CARTEL ON CANADIAN CONSUMERS
IMPACT OF CARTEL ON CANADIAN CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would suggest that the Prime Minister might check his records and perhaps report later in the day to the House concerning whether such independent counsel have in fact been appointed and are still being retained by the government on behalf of certain ministers and civil servants in connection with the uranium cartel combines investigation in Canada.
As my final question, would the Prime Minister indicate, since he sanctioned the various orders in council and regulations, and took other steps with respect to the activities of the uranium producers, including Crown corporations, during the period 1972 through 1978, whether he was ever aware of the implications such a cartel had for Canadian consumers, in short, that the price rigging, quota setting and other activities of this cartel were having an impact on Canadian consumers, and not only at present but in the future?

May 27, 1981
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: IMPACT OF CARTEL ON CANADIAN CONSUMERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I indicated yesterday in an answer to the House, the intent of these regulations was quite clear. It was to protect Canadian citizens and corporations from the extraterritorial effect of U.S. law. That was the intent of the regulations. If the competition bureau has uncovered anything which is otherwise illegal, then I imagine they will be reporting it and it will be in the hands of the attorney general. This I do not know.

subtopic: IMPACT OF CARTEL ON CANADIAN CONSUMERS
speechtext: Let us see the report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: IMPACT OF CARTEL ON CANADIAN CONSUMERS
speechtext: However, I made it quite clear that the intent of the regulations was to protect the Canadian uranium industry, and not in any sense to put pressure on the Canadian consumer. On the contrary, it was to keep alive a Canadian industry which was being very severely discriminated against by United States regulations respecting the free entry of Canadian products into their market.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also for the Prime Minister. It is clear that the methods of marketing utilized by the uranium cartel involved a scheme of bid rigging, and what happened is that there would be a true bidder designated by a secretariat in Paris, and a secondary sham bid. Senior Canadian officials participated in establishing the rules of the cartel, and the cabinet over which the Prime Minister presided implemented the regulations which gave effect to these artificially high prices. In light of this fact, how does the Prime Minister justify the marketing? Is it not just plain cheating and fraud on the purchasers of uranium?
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, this matter came before the House in great detail during past years. The situation is still exactly the same. Canada, along with several other countries producing uranium, took protective measures. We found it was our duty; we still believe it was our duty. I am surprised we do not have the support of the opposition to protect Canadian producers and workers against discriminatory measures taken in the United States.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

Oh, oh!

But in the last analysis the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General of Canada will have to make the decision.

subsubtopic: VIEW OF GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA ON FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance I should like to direct my question to the Prime Minister. It concerns the evidence given yesterday to the Senate Committee on National Finance by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Gerald Bouey. Governor Bouey indicated to the committee that he felt the Canadian economy was working at virtually full capacity, and that unemployment was still too low. He described the labour markets as being very tight in Canada.
Does the Prime Minister regard an economy which is working at around 80 per cent capacity as being full capacity? Does he share the view of the Governor of the Bank of Canada that unemployment right now is too low in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: VIEW OF GOVERNOR OF BANK OF CANADA ON FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I read hastily the statement prepared by Governor Bouey. I saw nowhere in it that he indicated unemployment was too low. If the hon. member has a quote, I would stand corrected, but I have not seen any such words from the mouth of the governor. Perhaps the hon. member read them in the press, but I do not believe he heard them from the governor.
As to operating near capacity, the hon. member knows the figures. In the last quarter of last year the economy was operating at a real growth rate of 8 per cent on a real basis. In this first quarter it is 6 per cent on a yearly basis. We do not know if these trends will continue. We do know they are very high growth rates, indeed very much higher than the growth rates in other industrialized countries. These growth rates have caused a fall in unemployment rates, not a rise.
May 27, 1981

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, when the transcript of the evidence of Governor Bouey is available, I think it will indicate that the governor said the labour markets were tight and that the economy needed to produce more slack before he felt the war on inflation would be won. In that light I would like to ask the Prime Minister, since we now have over 900,000 unemployed soldiers in the trench war on inflation and like some First World War general, Governor Bouey is saying, "Let us send another half million into the trenches in order to fight inflation", if it is his view, and the view of his government, that unemployment should increase. If that is the view, how high should unemployment go? Is the Prime Minister prepared to accept the policy of the Governor of the Bank of Canada in this regard, and will he come clean with the Canadian people and say just how much unemployment he thinks is necessary in order to fight this useless trench war against inflation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member asks if it is the view of the government or of the Governor of the Bank of Canada that unemployment should be higher. It is certainly not the view of the government, and I just challenged the hon. member to indicate where the governor had ever used such words. The hon. member tells me that when the transcript is available we will see. I suggest that the hon. member should come clean and tell us now that he is only fantasizing from headlines and not from words which were actually spoken.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister is an expert on fantasizing. I simply indicate to him that when the Governor of the Bank of Canada states that in his view labour markets are very tight and the economy is working at capacity, that means he thinks we have to reduce capacity in order to fight inflation, which means he thinks a higher rate of unemployment is acceptable.
Oh, oh!

Among other things Governor Bouey also said he thought that the government had made a mistake and that he had made a mistake in reducing interest rates in the period between April and July of last year. Since the government took great credit for the fact that interest rates went down during that period, and since it was regarded as an act of deliberate policy-in fact part of the genius of the Minister of Finance- I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he agrees with Governor Bouey that the government made a mistake in reducing interest rates at that time. Can the Prime Minister tell us whether it is his intention to reduce interest rates over time, or whether it is the intention of the government to maintain interest rates at the level which Governor Bouey
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to praise the government, but in all justice I cannot do it.
My question is for the Prime Minister. Last Thursday the shareholders of the CDC met at Winnipeg to re-elect a board of directors and to have their annual meeting. The government nominated four directors to the board, led by Maurice Strong, the Prime Minister's pet fixer, and three other Liberals. Is it correct that the deputy minister of finance, Mr. Ian Stewart, met with the board of directors of CDC previous to the shareholders' meeting, and advised them that the government wanted two other directors appointed, Mr. Joel Bell, the vice-president of Petro-Canada, and Mr. David Beatty, a former partner of Mr. Jim Coutts in the firm of Canada Consulting, that these two gentlemen also had to be appointed or the government would vote its shares to dismiss all of the directors of CDC if they did not carry out the government's wishes? Would the Prime Minister also explain the reasons for that kind of action, and would he agree to a public inquiry into the whole situation surrounding the Canada Development Corporation over the last month or so, its future direction, what will

The Prime Minister fails to understand the seriousness of this situation, and he did not answer my question. subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-LETTER WRITTEN BY MR. AXWORTHY RESPECTING CANADA COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this question of privilege has to do with a letter that was sent by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to the member of Parliament for Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Baker), which letter subsequently came into my possession and the possession of other members of this House. It involves a written misleading and false reply contained in that letter. I have to give Your Honour some background first.
Last summer of 1980 the government announced the Canada community development projects program for 198081. The total funding for that program for all of Canada was $105.5 million. The amount of the funding for the province of Newfoundland was $17,376 million and the funding was supposed to be spent in accordance with the level of unemployment in various areas of Canada.
Under that program the deadline for projects to be submitted if they were to receive approval for funding was September 29, 1980. If you put in an application from any district of the country after that date, under the guidelines sent out by the minister and his department it could not be considered for funding after that date. I will come back to the importance of that date in a few moments. As a matter of fact, I know of projects that were submitted two days after September 29, 1980 which the minister's office rejected and said could not be processed because they were late and outside the guidelines.

May 27, 1981

It was also part of the guidelines for the program that projects had to start by February 2, 1981. The guidelines were sent to every member of Parliament and widely publicized across the whole country.
During October, 1980, in Newfoundland the provincial boy scouts' council requested the seven members of Parliament for Newfoundland to allocate some of the funds for their districts to a project for the boy scouts that was going to be constructed in the district of Gander-Twillingate. The basis of their appeal was that this facility would benefit boy scouts all over Newfoundland and they needed the help of the MPs from all over Newfoundland to fund that project.
As a result I, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Rooney), the hon. member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons) and the minister for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) agreed to allocate $25,000 each from funds allocated to their districts to build this project in the district of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate. The project was a project of the provincial boy scouts council.
On October 23, for example, I received a letter from the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate thanking me for that co-operation. One Newfoundland member did not contribute, the hon. member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin).
In the fall or early winter of 1981 $2 million in additional funds were made available to the minister to spend on this program in whatever way he liked, in whatever political way he wished. A few weeks later, in February 1981, a further $4.9 million was made available secretly by the government to the minister to spend across Canada on these projects.

Madam Speaker, the relevance of all this will very soon become apparent.
There was $4.9 million made available, unknown to ordinary Canadians and members, in additional funding for this program for the minister to spend at his discretion. The minister decided to allocate $275,000 of that funding for the province of Newfoundland. Now I am coming to the relevancy and you will see that all this is relevant, Madam Speaker.
The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate apparently did not hear of any money being made available for his district, so he wrote the Minister of Employment and Immigration on February 26 asking whether additional funds were to be allocated to Gander-Twillingate under this program. The minister answered him in a letter dated April 14, 1981. In the mean-
Privilege-Mr. Crosbie
time, of the $275,000 allocated for Newfoundland the minister made $150,000 available to the district of Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador for a 1982 Winter Games Association, Incor-prated project 2855 MA9 submitted by the people of Labrador City-Wabush and signed by one Gordon Manstan. The application from that group was dated February 5, 1981. It was received by the department February 23, 1981, five months late-five months after the deadline for that project. Despite violating all these guidelines the Minister of Employment and Immigration allocated $150,000 to his colleague the Minister of National Revenue, for a project that did not meet the guidelines of the program at all. It may be a good project, but it should be funded from sports and recreation, or wherever, not in violation of the employment program.
In this letter, and I have a copy in my hand now, from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to his Liberal colleague, the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), he is responding to a letter of February 26. He tells him that his constituency received an allocation of $3 million originally, and then he goes on to say this in the third paragraph:
Federal constituencies in Newfoundland received $275,000 of the incremental funds which were distributed amongst the five constituencies which had transferred a portion of their initial allocations to your constituency.
There is not a word of truth in that paragraph because in the district of St. John's West not one cent was received of the $275,000 incremental funds to repay St. John's West for the contribution of $25,000 to the member of Parliament for Gander-Twillingate's boy scouts project. Not a cent of those funds went to the district represented in this House by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). Whether any of the other three districts got anything, I do not know, and no funding went to Gander-Twillingate. So, Madam Speaker-

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-LETTER WRITTEN BY MR. AXWORTHY RESPECTING CANADA COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, it is not about that at all. My question of privilege has to do with a letter sent by a minister to a member of Parliament which contains false and misleading information and which, therefore, interfered with and breached his privileges as a member of this House, breached the privileges of this House generally and that of every other member who was sent a copy of the letter. It has no connection with the violating of the guidelines of the program.
I am giving the background so that this letter can be understood, and this is based on a precedent of this House to which I will come in a few minutes and in which a prima facie case of privilege was found by Mr. Speaker Jerome in 1978.

May 27, 1981
Privilege-Mr. Crosbie
Just to finish this background, how did the hon. member for St. John's West get a copy of this letter containing false and misleading information from the Minister of Employment and Immigration? A copy was sent to me by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate with a note dated April 16 which reads as follows:
John,
As you can see by the attached letter your constituency received an additional amount of money to compensate for your constituency contribution to the boy scout camp.
Congratulations!
The hon. member was congratulating me for receiving this additional funding. He was pleased to see that I got this additional funding for making $25,000 available to the district of Gander-Twillingate during the fall.
What is the nature of the complaint? The outline of the facts here shows, of course, that the program was violated. The guidelines were ignored by one cabinet minister listening to a supplication from another cabinet minister. Dozens of projects were turned down as being late. Five months later one was allowed, and $150,000 went to it, although it did not meet the guidelines of the program at all. That was to the detriment of many dozens of other projects submitted in Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador and all over Newfoundland, but that is not the complaint. The complaint is that the minister, having done that, wrote a letter to a member of Parliament, a colleague of his in his own party, and deliberately gave him wrong information.

speechtext: False information.

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-LETTER WRITTEN BY MR. AXWORTHY RESPECTING CANADA COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
False information. In other words, he was saying to the member of Parliament for Gander-Twillingate, "You didn't get any of this $275,000 because I took that $275,000 for Newfoundland and repaid the five districts that helped you out in your boy scouts project." That is what the program means. We have two members in this House who can testify to the falseness of that information, and the minister had to know it was false.
What about the precedents? I have a motion here that I am ready to move. I am fully aware that the function of the Speaker is to decide whether there is a prima facie case of privilege or not, and if she finds that, the matter then has to be debated and voted on by the House.
I want to refer Your Honour to a recent precedent. If you look at Hansard for November 3, 1978 at page 111, you will see a similar kind of complaint made by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence). There was a letter from a minister of the Crown which misled the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland several years earlier. It was not even in the same year; it was in a different Parliament. The minister of the Crown had sent him a letter with misleading and false information and, in turn, the hon. member for that district had misled his constituent. There was a written misleading and false reply sent to that member which directly affected his capabilities and attitudes in the House with respect to his duties as a member of Parliament.
This program is one of the more important programs, I can assure you, in Atlantic Canada where employment is very, very badly needed and where there are thousands and thousands of projects put forward by communities and groups. Nothing could be more important in creating employment in our rural areas. Yet we were given misleading and false replies by the minister as to how the funds were being spent.
As it was said then, and I repeat now, I should be able as a member of Parliament, as should the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate, both in and out of this House, to trust the word of a minister of the Crown. Surely if a minister writes us a letter stating that certain things have happened and that certain funds have been distributed in a certain way, we are expected to trust his word as a member of Parliament and minister of the Crown. If we cannot trust his word, the whole system collapses. That is what affects the privileges of this House and members of Parliament. We should be able to trust the word of such members.
I will not read long citations from May. I presume Your Honour will be looking them up because this is a very serious question of privilege. The nineteenth edition of May at page 67 deals with what constitutes privilege:
The distinctive mark of a privilege is its ancillary character. The privileges of Parliament are rights which are "absolutely necessary for the due execution of its powers". They are enjoyed by individual members, because the House cannot perform its functions without unimpeded use of the services of its members; and by each House for the protection of its members and the vindication of its own authority and dignity.
We as members need to be protected from any suggestion or any possibility that other members of this House or ministers of the Crown will deliberately mislead us. If we do not have that kind of assurance and if we cannot be absolutely sure of that, then this whole system of Parliament founders.
I want to refer Your Honour to page 141, which deals with acts or conduct constituting a contempt of Parliament and an abuse of our rights:
It is a breach of privilege to present or cause to be presented to either House or to committees of either House forged, falsified or fabricated documents with intent to deceive such House or committees or to subscribe the names of other persons or fictitious names to documents-

Yes, the hon. member has that right, and that is what he should do, but he should not raise a question of privilege about it. Of course the hon. member has the right to criticize actions of ministers or the government and to ask questions about what a particular minister has done, about which the hon. member might have a grievance. I have heard the hon. member for more than 15 minutes and I must interrupt him now, because if he has not proved to me in the course of 15 minutes that he has a question of privilege, I do not think he will be able to do so in the next five minutes.
The letter and the precedent to which he alludes are quite different. That precedent has to do with a letter which had been improperly drafted by the RCMP and which they admitted had been improperly drafted, and which probably allegedly impeded the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) in performing his duties in the House. So that precedent does not apply; it is a completely different type of letter.
The hon. member probably has a grievance, he wants to levy some kind of criticism of the minister in question and he is quite entitled to do that, but not under the guise of a question of privilege. I must therefore rule that he does not have a prima facie case of privilege.

Madam Speaker, my question of privilege, I am thankful to say, is not on the same point although the similarity of what I am complaining about will be clear.
1 delivered this morning to your office, Madam Speaker, a statement of my question of privilege and I intend now to speak to you and the House on it in order to enlarge somewhat on my question of privilege. It involves an attempt to change the wording in the minutes that reflect what happened in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
At a meeting of that committee on May 14, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) gave an opening statement of which he appeared to be reading part and ad libbing part. He did not circulate a copy of the text from which he was reading although he did at a later meeting circulate a copy of a NATO press release.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. McKINNON-ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO ALTER RECORD OF COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Order, please. I am very sorry but the hon. member's question of privilege relates to deliberations which took place in a standing committee. The hon. member knows that deliberations taking place there cannot be dealt with in the House until such time as the committee reports back to the House. Therefore, I am afraid I have to advise him that the place to deal with his particular question of privilege would be in the standing committee and not in the House.

subtopic: MR. McKINNON-ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO ALTER RECORD OF COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
There are two points I would like to make on that, Madam Speaker. First, I know of no method whereby the chairman of the standing committee could refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Second, part of the offence did take place in this House on May 20 when the minister misled the House during part of the same nefarious conduct that I am complaining about. I was hindered in my duties as a member of Parliament by a misleading and untrue statement that he made in the first part of his answer to my first question that day.
Now, if I may proceed, Madam Speaker? When speaking of possible NATO commitments outside of the recognized NATO boundaries, the minister said:
Canada has made a new commitment to deploy its NATO forces outside the normal NATO treaty area.
I was rather surprised and said that I hoped the minutes of the committee would reflect his ad libs as well as his written statement. On May 15 the unedited transcript of the minutes were sent to my office and it confirmed the remarks that I heard, which were:
Canada has made a new commitment to deploy its NATO forces outside the normal NATO treaty area.
In the second meeting of the same committee the minister, in reply to questions from two Liberal MPs, said there was no
new commitment. 1 assume that he was contradicting himself as he sometimes does. He made no comment that his remarks of May 14 were in error.

Now, the hon. member asks how that can be dealt with because that committee does not have the authority to refer the matter to another standing committee.
The procedure would be that if the standing committee found the minister had tampered-allegedly tampered-or had done whatever the hon. member says he has done, the committee would report such action to the House. Then the House would be able to deal with it by referring it to another committee in order for the committee to pronounce on that particular action. This would be the procedure, and this is the way to deal with that kind of matter.
If the hon. member can state his case without arguing that he is not satisfied with the answer given the House, I can hear him.

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-SECURITY MEASURES ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question of privilege arises from an incident which occurred at approximately 6.35 p.m. last evening when my wife and I were leaving the Centre Block of the Parliament Buildings to proceed along our direct and usual way in exiting from Parliament Hill. My wife was driving our vehicle, which clearly bore House of Commons special licence plates as issued by the province of Ontario with the customary prefix MHC. I was sitting in the front of the car on the passenger side.
Before proceeding further, I would like emphatically to state that nothing I intend to say, or will say, is meant to detract from what I am sure we all agree are the very necessary stringent security regulations protecting the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), particularly in light of the recent incidents involving President Reagan in the United States and His Holiness Pope Jean Paul II in Rome. Also, before proceeding further may I say to you, Madam Speaker, that I realize the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) raised a question of privilege a few days ago on which you gave a ruling yesterday. I hope I will have the opportunity to
illustrate that my question of privilege is sufficiently different from the one raised by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants and that it cannot be said that I am speaking on something about which you have already ruled.
I would now like to return to the incident in question. As we were signalling a left turn to proceed toward the members' entrance of the Centre Block, with the intention of proceeding down the hill to Wellington Street, an RCMP constable somewhat frantically rushed out from our left and ordered my wife to come to a full stop and then to turn around and proceed in the opposite direction at once. I got out of the car and asked the officer what this was all about. He replied, "I cannot tell you, just move at once; 1 have my orders". I then identified myself as a member of Parliament travelling with my wife-

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-SECURITY MEASURES ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext: You are a Canadian like anyone else.

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-SECURITY MEASURES ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext: I am a Canadian like what, did you say? If hon. members opposite will stop their silly shenanigans, I might be able to proceed.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant
subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-SECURITY MEASURES ON PARLIAMENT HILL

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-SECURITY MEASURES ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
I am telling you, Madam Speaker, they started them when they started as a party and they will continue them until they cease to exist as a party, which may be sooner than they like to think.
To get on with my question of privilege, Madam Speaker, having identified myself as a member of Parliament travelling with my wife I offered identification and again demanded to know why my exit was being impeded from the Hill. Again I drew attention to my MHC licence plate as identification and offered to produce my House of Commons identification. The RCMP constable replied, "I am not permitted to answer your questions. How do I know you are really an MP? Move out."

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-SECURITY MEASURES ON PARLIAMENT HILL

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-SECURITY MEASURES ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when I finish outlining the incident, 1 believe that will become apparent. I am approaching the crucial point of the incident.
1 asked the RCMP constable if there was something wrong here. I asked, "Has there been an accident? Is someone coming out of the members' door?" I asked him if no member was allowed to go in that door. He replied, "I have orders. I am not allowed to say whether anyone is coming or going at that door. Hurry up and move."
It was at this point that I noticed that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) was standing on the sidewalk adjacent to the members' entrance along with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien). I observed that everything on the Hill had been brought to a complete standstill by the police, including the stoppage of the House of Commons buses which were proceeding to the Hill. I cannot prove this, but I would presume that the buses carried members of Parliament who were proceeding to the Hill to perform their duties as members of Parliament. Of course, the public were stopped as well.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice were obviously not engaged in a serious conversation but in a conversation which could have waited until later. By his actions the Prime Minister was holding up the entrance to-and I emphasize that point-and exit from the building. He was guffawing and giggling and the Minister of Justice was also doing a good job of guffawing and giggling. I feel that if the Prime Minister requires security, and I agree that he does, he should not take advantage of that security by tying up all of Parliament Hill for the purpose of giggling and guffawing and holding up everyone else who has plans, as members, to come into the building to carry out their functions in the House or to attend committee meetings, etc., or even to leave the buildings to speak at a function, as we are obligated to do as part of our duty as members of Parliament.
I contend that the Prime Minister, not the RCMP-I do not fault the RCMP for this at all since I feel they were carrying out their orders-was misusing his office and the security which has been and should be afforded to him in a way which was actually impeding the work of any number of members of Parliament. While I saw some members in the area, I am not sure how many there were at that particular time. I did not actually go around to the buses to see how many members of Parliament were on them.
This was a disgusting and disgraceful display. If it is still going on, and I have no reason to believe that it is not, I believe it should be fully investigated and that it should stop. If the Prime Minister wants to leave the Hill with protection, why does he not simply go to his car and leave instead of standing around and impeding the duties of members of Parliament? That is what he was doing and there is no question about it.
Privilege-Mr. Cossitt

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I feel that the Prime Minister of Canada was, in effect, impeding the ability of members of this House to perform their duties as members. I would not criticize the right hon. gentleman if it was something crucial which required him to be where he was. The silly part of it is that he was simply giggling and guffawing and making jokes on the sidewalk. He caused everything to come to a standstill. I think it is a disgrace.
If you do find that I have a question of privilege, Madam Speaker, I would like to reserve my right to move the appropriate motion.

Madam Speaker, I have a question of privilege which I can state very briefly, but it is nonetheless one of great importance to me and to the people of Nova Scotia. It arises from remarks made during the question period by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) and repeated indirectly by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
The remarks were to the effect that I asked the government and the Prime Minister to refer to the Supreme Court of Canada the question of the ownership of offshore resources; that is to say, the ownership of the minerals, hydrocarbons and the submarine lands off the coasts of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. The remarks of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice relate to a debate which took place in the House on May 20, 1981, in which this matter was raised. I said then what I say now.
The Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister misinterpreted the nature of that exchange in that I had said that this question ought to be referred to the Supreme Court only if the Prime Minister and his government were unwilling to continue the political action of negotiating with the provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland over the settlement of the ownership of those resources. 1 want to say to Your Honour, to all hon. members of this House and to the people of Canada that this question of ownership of offshore resources is just as important to the people of Nova Scotia as it is to the other provinces.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government's National Energy Program because of the substantial adverse impact it has had on energy development in Canada, and on those parts of the economy which supply goods and services to the oil and gas industry.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank hon. members opposite for their patience in waiting for my speech. I want to assure them that, like a good wine, my speech has improved with age!
Yesterday we debated Bill C-57. During the opening speeches on that bill we discussed amendments to delete the production tax and the excise tax on natural gas, principally because of the damage it is doing in the area of supply, the area of energy development and the deadlock that has caused the megaprojects to be put on hold, as well as the consequent very dangerous exposure which this country faces in view of the increasing reliance on the Middle East.
As I said yesterday, these taxes are at the heart of the problems that we will encounter in the years ahead. But there is another side to this issue, and that is the immediate impact of the government's energy program on the economy today. It is a very visible side of this issue. As I have said in the past in this House, 139 rigs have left the country since October 28; drilling activity is down in excess of 50 per cent this year compared to the same period last year, and in addition land sales on petroleum properties have declined about 70 per cent. All this is having a ripple effect throughout the entire economy. It is that aspect of the energy program that I wish to debate today.
We on this side have discussed the effects of this energy program on individuals, businesses, different sectors of the economy, not just in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, but also in parts of eastern Canada which are important suppliers to the oil and gas industry. Many of us in this House met with representatives of the oil service industry. They told us about small companies of five, ten, 15, 30 and 40 people and stated categorically that if no changes are made in the situation as it is today, about half of them will be out of business within six months and about 70 per cent will be out of business within one year.
A very urgent problem faces us, Mr. Speaker, and that is the reason for the motion we are debating today. The motion stands in my name but I am proud to make it on behalf of the many people in my party who have felt directly the concerns of the people so severely affected by the program brought forward by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), on October 28-the energy program.
9988

May 27, 1981
National Energy Program
Let me just read the motion quickly:
That this House condemns the government's National Energy Program because of the substantia] adverse impact it has had on energy development in Canada, and on those parts of the economy which supply goods and services to the oil and gas industry.
As I mentioned earlier, some of the service companies have been to Ottawa to discuss the very real problems that affect them, the people who work for them and the people in their communities. I should like to refer briefly to some of these. One individual had seven leases of rental equipment cancelled outright with the resultant loss of $500,000 to him and to his small company when the equipment had to be returned to the bank. Another person, also in the equipment rental business, who one year ago employed 26 people, now employs 11 people. There is a contractor who, in 1980, employed 50 people but this year employs only 20. Another construction company had 137 people in 1980 and now has only 27.
We would not ordinarily think of hotel owners being in the oil and gas business, but they accommodate the people who work on the rigs. A particular hotel owner had 68 employees in 1980; now he has 38, the loss of business being directly attributed to the National Energy Program.
I should like to refer to a survey conducted by my colleague the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) on companies in his constituency. Ele asked: "Has your firm experienced an actual reduction in financial activity in the last six months?" Mr. Speaker, 82 per cent replied that they had. The average amount of the decrease was 41 per cent, so it is a substantial decrease and it is much greater than in other parts of the economy.
The next question was: "Has the change in financial activity been a direct result of the National Energy Program?" About 50 per cent of the companies canvassed responded to the questionnaire-and that is a high number, Mr. Speaker-and 88 per cent replied that the change had been a direct result of the NEP.
About 55 per cent of the respondents are involved directly in the oil and gas industry. I should point out that 81 per cent of the companies are 100 per cent Canadian owned. This is the result of the Canadianization program that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has introduced.
Unemployment has increased in the riding of Peace River. Last year employment was about 4,000 people-3,964. This year it is down to 3,065, a decrease of about 22 per cent.
Finally, "Could you indicate the amount of capital you spent and what you plan to spend within the Peace River constituency in the following years?". In 1979-80, it was around $35 million or $37 million. In 1981-82, these companies are projecting about $18.5 million, a decline of about 50 per cent. There are very real indications of the disastrous effect this policy has had on individual business, small business, Canadian-owned business, businesses that are the heart of the economy of this country.
Let me also refer to the effects of this on companies in eastern Canada. There is a very direct impact. The Alberta government, in conjunction with companies in the industry, did a survey on the economic impact of the Alsands and Cold Lake projects. The purpose of this was to show that the economic activity generated by these projects in Alberta was about 42 per cent, and in Ontario and Quebec the total amount was 35 per cent; a little over 25 per cent in Ontario and a little over 9 per cent in Quebec. Therefore, these projects have a very direct impact in eastern Canada.
The megaprojects have been put on the back burner for some considerable length of time as a result of the discussions and disagreements that have taken place between the Alberta government and the federal government. We are at a very serious point in time where these projects just may not go ahead, in particular because of the deadlock between these two levels of government and because of the effect of the taxes, specifically the production tax, on these projects. In addition, the pricing schedule of the energy program has been stated quite categorically to be insufficient to bring forward the investment necessary.
Foster Associates did another broader impact study on conventional and megaproject investment as it relates to the rest of Canada. Of every dollar that is spent on both sides of the business, the megaprojects and conventional projects, 42 cents is spent in Ontario, 13 cents in Quebec, 16 cents in other provinces and 29 cents in Alberta. Therefore, this is not just an Alberta problem, or a British Columbia problem, but a Canadian problem. That is the point we want to make in the debate today.
The Foster Associates study went on to say that for every job created in Alberta by these projects, two additional jobs are created in the rest of Canada. The impact on the rest of Canada is not as massive as it is in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Other of my colleagues will be discussing those specifically today. I would like to talk about some of the broader elements of the slowdown in the industry so that we can have a better understanding in this House of the impact of the policies the government is following.
Ralph Hedlin Associates completed a very intensive report entitled "Some Implications of the National Energy Program on Ontario and Quebec manufacturers". Let me just refer to the broad range of industries that are affected by the National Energy Program: the rubber industry, steel industry, wire rope, structural steel, fabricated pipe, boilers and pressure vessels, valves, turbines, pumps, controls, electrical equipment, transportation, measurement and control equipment. I would imagine that covers well over 75 per cent of the total manufacturing range of industries in this country. It is a very broad problem that we face.
Let us look at the compressor industry, one of the industries that is hardest hit. One firm in this industry estimates that losses of $40 million are due to cancelled, reduced or delayed orders. Another firm reports a fall-off from $17 million in sales about a year ago to $1.7 million, a 90 per cent drop in
May 27, 1981

sales in the two-month period of January and February. One company reports that under normal business conditions they would bid on 30 to 40 projects per month. Now they are bidding on three to four in the oil and gas industry. This is a serious situation that is growing worse daily.
Let us look at the rubber industry. They had anticipated orders of about $22 million for the Alsands project. These are delayed, I guess you could say indefinitely because the minister has been unable to make any progress as a result of the decisions he has taken in the negotiations with the Alberta government. They attribute these delays directly to the National Energy Program.
One structural steel company predicted about $100 million in potential business for western Canada. This is now on hold as a result of the program. One fabricated pipe manufacturer, who unfortunately had expanded production facilities prior to the National Energy Program, is now operating far below capacity with very substantial interest rates to maintain, as a result not just of the slowdown in the energy industry but the very high interest rate policy of this government.
Finally, in the electrical industry one company had planned to establish a research and development capability but it has now put that on hold pending resolution of the energy deadlock in this country. With the uncertainty and the direct impact of this energy policy, there is substantial loss of economic activity and loss of potential to the economy of this country that must be addressed very quickly or we will face very serious consequences throughout this country.
Let me draw some conclusions from the Fledlin study which I believe it important for members of this House to consider. The first is obviously the very broad relationship of the oil and gas industry to the total manufacturing economy of this country, not just in western Canada but all of Canada. This is a very important relationship that we must learn to better understand in this House.
Second, the immediate impact that the Hedlin study has observed is not nearly as much as the medium or longer-term impact, as the over-all result of this loss of business starts to affect orders that will be lost, sales that will be lost, lost employment opportunities as well as investment opportunities or the creation of new plant and equipment which generates economic activity in this country.
The key is that the next 12 months is a critical period for all of these industries. That is the period during which the direct impact will be felt by the country. If the megaprojects, the Alsands and Cold Lake projects, are delayed, the impact on this country will be disastrous, not just in lost supply so important to us in 1990, but in the economic activity that we need so desperately in this country today.
The intransigencies of the minister and the provocative approach that he and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took to these oil negotiations last year at this time have resulted in the most serious government-induced slowdown in our economy that I think anybody in this House can remember, and
National Energy Program
perhaps I could say it is the most serious government-induced slowdown of our economy in history.
The Alberta reaction which resulted in cutbacks and putting these megaprojects on hold was a predictable reaction. In face of the way the minister and the Prime Minister conducted the negotiations last summer, it is clear there were few options the government of Alberta had when the energy program finally came out and showed, if you can believe it, a less satisfactory offer to the provinces than had been offered to them back in July. It was no surprise. I think anybody could have predicted it and we were predicting it in this House prior to the energy program, if there was not a more realistic approach when the energy program was finally brought down.
Today the outlook for the Canadian economy is not good. We had unexpected strength in the fourth quarter of last year and the first quarter this year, but with the high interest rate policy that this government has maintained throughout this whole period and with increasing interest rates, it is clear to me that the economy cannot stand that sort of stress and still maintain any degree of economic growth. The future is very cloudy indeed, and we need desperately this energy development to be brought forward to take up the slack in this economy.
I am not the only person saying that. If you read economic reports, including the one of the Economic Council of Canada, you will see stated very clearly in the last report that the key hope for this economy is energy development in this country.
Let me refer briefly to a statement made by the Governor of the Bank of Canada yesterday when he was before the committee in the other place. He said:
-a settlement of energy disputes probably ought to be given the highest priority in economic policy these days ... I think the settlement might very well help us on the exchange rate and might improve the investment climate.
I believe you know, Mr. Speaker, that the Governor of the Bank of Canada is a very subdued and soft-spoken individual, but I think that is a very powerful message he has given us to date. What he is saying to us is that because there is uncertainty about future energy development in this country in face of the real energy problems the world faces, there has been downward pressure on the Canadian dollar-the exchange rate, to use his words.
He also indicated previously in his testimony that if there was not that pressure on the exchange rate he would have an opportunity to reduce the level of interest rates in this country. Quite clearly, the direction the Governor of the' Bank of Canada has followed is in maintaining an interest rate policy which clearly has an eye to the level of the Canadian dollar, because if the dollar falls further than it has to date it will generate further inflationary pressures in this country.
Let us be quite clear. When you cut through it all what we are referring to is jobs-jobs of individual Canadians in small businesses, medium-sized businesses and very large businesses. This is most visible in the province of Alberta but we are starting to see it more and more from statements being made in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

May 27, 1981
National Energy Program
Let us not forget that last November and December we on this side of the House, as well as many other observers in the country, warned the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that the policy, if followed through, would result in the disasters that are starting to fall around us right now. We did predict oil drilling activities and we did predict the drop in land sales. Now this is a fact.
How long is the minister going to sit there nodding his head saying yes, yes, yes, when we talk about the broader economic effects of this policy and do nothing about it? The statistics we see today clearly demonstrate that we knew what we were talking about in November and December, and the statistics of later on this year will prove that we know what we are talking about today. Very few people in this country disagree with us.
Let me refer to another element which I think involves an important message which I am receiving from people in my constituency and others who are directly affected, and that is the oil brain drain. This is quietly happening today, Mr. Speaker. Canada is not an island unto itself in energy development. We have to be conscious of what is happening in the rest of the world. We are part of a broad, worldwide oil and gas industry. I do not think there is another country in the world which has taken the approach that Canada has to oil development. Other countries are aggressively pursuing exploration and production of oil and gas. They are valuable commodities to these countries, so we have a competitive situation here. Our young men and women are being drawn away from Canada because of uncertainty and the lack of jobs in this country, jobs which are available for them in spades in many other countries of the world, most particularly in the United States because it is right at our doorstep.
Mr. Gerry Maier, chairman and chief executive officer of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Co., recently made a speech on this subject. He said:
As long as Canadian energy policy results in cash flow cutbacks and reduced profits for the industry, the temptation to move to greener pastures will remain strong.
He goes on to say:
In the U.S.A. reducing dependence on foreign petroleum has become a virtual crusade, and Canadian recruits are being welcomed with open arms.
The prospects clearly are better in other parts of the world. The uncertainty which has been created by this energy program in Canada is pushing our technologists, our highly technical experts, out of the country to other parts of the world. The industry and the governments in these other countries have accepted as a common goal the need for greater production. We must accept that today or we will lose more of our highly technical people.
The result of this will be that when these projects are to be developed the people we need to bring them on stream will not be available. What that means is that we will get the second best talent, which will result in longer times to bring the project on and it will result in mistakes. The net result of that is that the consumer in this country will pay more for energy
developments that could be under way today if this government had any sense.
In face of these clear signs of deterioration, whether it is from conventional drilling, delay in the megaprojects or from the oil brain drain, it is hard to understand the complacency of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He is saying they have a majority in the House of Commons and they are going to ram this program through. They do not have to listen to anybody. They can build the monument to Marc Lalonde.
Another statement he has made which disturbs me tremendously is that if they are going to get beaten in the next election they should get beaten by something they really believe in; not what the people want but what they, Marc Lalonde and other members of the government, feel is important to their small little world.

He must learn, he must pay attention and he must be sensitive to what is happening in the rest of the world. He must pay attention to the decisions which are being made by people in the industry and by individuals who are going to those green pastures to which Mr. Maier referred. If the minister does not do these things, his Utopia will force Canadians to accept lower living standards, less economic security and a much more uncertain and cloudy future than we see even today.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that we finally got around to debating this motion which the Progressive Conservative members of the opposition surely deemed very important and very urgent, but which they even came close to stranding completely because of the altogether unfounded questions of privilege raised during a full hour by various members opposite.

For an hour we listened to a number of frivolous Conservative questions of privilege and points of order. The hon. member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) tried to back away from a position he impressed upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a week or two ago. Having reflected upon his attitude at first, the hon. member tried to back away from the position he took in this House. As the hon. member himself
May 27, 1981

said, the record will speak for itself. It is there for everyone to see.
[ Translation]
The motion before the House today reads very simply as follows, and I quote:
That this House condemns the government's National Energy Program because of the substantial adverse impact it has had on energy development in Canada, and on those parts of the economy which supply goods and services to the oil and gas industry.
If the Progressive Conservative members of the opposition had the courage of their convictions, they would have drafted a much clearer and much simpler motion. They would have said quite simply that the Progressive Conservative Party urges the government to raise consumer prices so as to give more money to the oil industry and to the producing provinces. Basically that is what the Conservative members have been advocating here and there and everywhere in the country, and we had the best example of that earlier from the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the Progressive Conservative opposition. In fact, what the Progressive Conservative Party is doing, and I quote, it "condemns the National Energy Program" as a whole. I see Conservative members opposite, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) who nods his head in agreement. It is important that Canadians know what the Progressive Conservative members object to when they say: We reject the National Energy Program. What they reject, Mr. Speaker, is a whole series of measures whose aim is Canada's self-sufficiency by 1990; what they reject is a whole series of measures to ensure that that industry will be controlled and owned by Canadians by 1990; what they reject is a price system which will be fair to consumers and to the various regions of the country as well as to the Canadian government and the government of the producing provinces. That is what the Progressive Conservative members reject. They should have the courage of their convictions. The National Energy Program provides for billions of dollars in grants to help Canadian consumers improve energy conservation through the Canadian Home Insulation Program, for instance, in which we pay half the cost of insulation up to $500 for each home. That is what the Progressive Conservative members reject. Similarly they reject measures to promote the replacement of petroleum by other forms of energy, something which must be done as quickly as possible because that is what will make Canadians self-sufficient in the short term. Thanks to the measures I announced on Monday, Mr. Speaker, we will be able to reduce oil consumption in Canada by 300,000 barrels a day. Canadian consumers will be eligible for up to $800 for each home to convert their oil heating system to a heating system operating on gas, electricity, wood, propane gas, solar energy or other forms of energy. That is what the Conservatives are condemning and rejecting. Let them have the courage of their opinions, let them stand up and be counted! The Canadian consumers will know how to judge their position on this subject.
National Energy Program
What else are they rejecting? They are rejecting the extension of the gas pipeline for the citizens of Quebec and the maritime provinces, which is an integral part of the National Energy Program.
