subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: So when the Conservative party puts a motion condemning the National Energy Program globally as they are doing in this debate, let us remember what they are condemning.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Fifty dollars to Mexico, SI5 to Alberta, that is what we are condemning.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
What I would like to cover more specifically is some points raised by the hon. member.

I believe that it is important, Mr. Speaker, to recall once again what it is that the Conservatives are opposing. What
they oppose is the National Energy Program as a whole, that is a good program for the Canadian consumers, a good program for Canadian ownership and Canadian control of this industry, and a program which will ensure energy self-sufficiency by 1990, which means that we shall no longer have to import foreign oil.
The Conservatives' answer would be to increase consumer prices and give more money to the corporations and the producing provinces even though in no other federal system in the world producing provinces receive as much as they do in Canada, and this under the National Energy Program. [English]
Now, the spokesman for the official opposition has depicted a very gloomy picture of the situation and I would like to draw to his attention a few facts. I will begin with what is happening in the Canada lands, Mr. Speaker. These lands are the exclusive responsibility of the Government of Canada, and if any blame is to be attributed, you cannot parcel it out. If something goes wrong in the Canada lands, the responsibility is that of the Government of Canada. However, if something good happens there, then the Government of Canada should get the credit. And what have we seen? The hon. member talks about the oil and gas industry. I would urge the official opposition to look at the oil industry in global terms, not just to look at Alberta and say that that is the end of it. Look at the situation in Saskatchewan, British Columbia and the Canada lands.
What is the situation in the Canada lands, Mr. Speaker? Well, I have no doubt that the Conservatives do not know what was spent there last year. Total expenditures by the oil and gas industry in the Canada lands last year was $345 million. And after the National Energy Program was announced in 1981, Mr. Speaker, how much is the industry going to spend there? It is going to spend $630 million, almost double what it spent last year. Then we go to next year and the year after. The forecast for 1982 is $880 million, and for 1983 it is $1,035 billion. That is the kind of action taking place in the Canada lands with the oil and gas industry. The Tories will not talk about that, they do not know any better. They like to believe the stories they are being told by some spokesmen for the industry and they do not want to look at the whole forest; they look at a few trees and knock their heads against them and refuse to see what is happening in the industry.
What is happening in the provincial lands? Well, I will not quote internal statistics because they will be challenged as being inaccurate; I will quote the opposition's preferred source, namely the industry magazines, such as Oilweek, for one, which I am sure is known if not read by some members on the other side, and what do we see there? They talk about wells disappearing or a small number of wells being drilled. Well, let us face it, we have a situation in this country where we have had a surplus of natural gas, and that has been going on for quite a while. People recognized this well before the National Energy Program was brought in, Mr. Speaker. That program had nothing to do with capped wells in Alberta or in other
May 27, 1981

provinces. They were there well before the NEP was announced, so much so that a spokesman for the gas industry said, well before the program was announced, that there would be a very substantial decline in drilling activity in western Canada in 1981. This is what the oil and gas journal said in quoting the executive director of the Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors before the NEP came into being. He said that no more than 5,000 wells would be drilled in Canada in 1981 compared with 8,300 wells in 1980, a drop of 40 per cent. That is not the government's policy, not the government's decision and not the National Energy Program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Read the rest of the quote.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
It is a fact that the Canadian Association of Oilwell Drilling Contractors stated, before the National Energy Program was announced, that because of a surplus of natural gas they would have a very drastic reduction in the number of wells drilled in this country in 1981 and, significantly, that is what has happened.
What do we see in Oilweekl Comparing the first quarter of 1981 with the first quarter of 1980 we see that the number of wells in development for natural gas has gone down. There is no surprise there. That was foreseen by the industry at least a year ago. Development wells are down from 641 to 457. And we see, in spite of the gloomy stories we hear from the opposition, that the number of exploration and development wells for oil has not gone down, Mr. Speaker, but has increased. Oil exploration wells went up in the first quarter from 162 to 253, according to Oilweek. Oil development wells have gone up from 284 to 400 and therefore, the total for oil has gone up from 446 to 653, over 200 more in the first quarter of 1981 compared to the first quarter of 1980. If you add all the wells together, including the gas wells, you end up with a larger number of wells in the first quarter of 1981 than in the first quarter of 1980. It went up from 2,004 to 2,235. These are the statistics, the facts, the reality of what is happening.
The situation for natural gas is indeed serious and one we have had to live with, as I said, well before the National Energy Program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Does the minister not realize that the figures he is quoting are the result of budgets established well before the National Energy Program, and that we are now just coming to the time when there will be a downturn? Surely he has the intelligence to understand that.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Order, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the time taken up for this point of order will be deducted from my time. There are so many inaccuracies and wrong statements made by the opposition that I will need all my time to answer them. We are not talking about previous budgets; we are talking about the first quarter of 1981-
National Energy Program

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: But it is a result of previous budgets.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
-which is several months after the October 28 budget came into effect. These are the facts as put out by Oilweek.
Obviously there are some problems. I indicated that as far as the Canada lands are concerned, we are seeing more activity under the National Energy Program than we have ever seen before. This is taking place, thanks to the National Energy Program. It benefits oil and gas companies, mainly Canadian gas companies. For the first time in the history of that industry, junior Canadian companies are involved in exploration.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: In the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: They are involved in exploration on the east coast and in the Arctic, which did not happen before. Also this is thanks to the National Energy Program. Most of those companies are from Calgary and Alberta.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Like Mobil!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
There are problems in some areas. After having indicated the areas where the federal government alone is responsible, I would like to indicate that there are problems in some provinces.
I would like to say a word about those provinces because while we are exclusively responsible for the Canada lands, everyone recognizes the provincial governments are getting the largest share of the benefits. They have responsibility as well as the national government when it comes to provincial lands. As a matter of fact, they like to claim that it is all theirs, but when it comes to paying their contribution or their share of the costs, they are not so eager.
Let me look at the situation in some provinces. If we look at the situation in Saskatchewan, for instance, we see royalties in the province which are higher than in any other province in Canada. We have a situation where some of those wells are being closed at the present time. I am sure the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) will want to talk about this. Some of those wells are being closed, but why? It is because of the excessively high royalties in the province of Saskatchewan. The royalties are higher than in any other province, royalties which the industry itself is blaming for the current closing down of a large number of wells in that province.
I hope the government of Saskatchewan will reflect upon this and realize that it must do something about this. What is the situation in Saskatchewan? Saskatchewan royalties are twice as high as Alberta's on the production of an average well; they are twice as high as those of its neighbouring province.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: So what?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
But our production is three times as low.

May 27, 1981
National Energy Program

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
For an average well in Saskatchewan producing about 30 barrels per day, the royalty on old oil is 51 per cent in Saskatchewan and 24 per cent in Alberta. Lower rate producers are hit even harder. A ten-barrel per day well pays 37 per cent royalty on old oil in Saskatchewan and only 8 per cent in Alberta.
The hon. member for Assiniboia can complain as much as he wants but those figures indicate clearly that if those wells were in Alberta, they would be still producing. They are being closed down at the present time because of the excessive royalties the government of Saskatchewan has imposed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Speak louder.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Now I would like to turn to British Columbia. We have heard a lot of noise from the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) earlier. What is the situation in British Columbia? Gas pricing in British Columbia is lower for the producer than it is in Alberta. The producer in British Columbia receives about $1.45 per thousand cubic feet for old gas after export adjustments. In Alberta the same producer receives $2.62. This is under the same National Energy Program. The situation in British Columbia has nothing to do with the National Energy Program. It has to do with the Socred government there and the type of decisions that government has taken. It is not the National Energy Program that is the cause of the difficulties in the industry in British Columbia at the present time. This has been repeated over and over again by the industry when representatives appeared before the British Columbia Utilities Commission.
I left Alberta to the last. Certainly Alberta has some problems. We have met with the service industries; many of them came from Alberta. Certainly these people attract our sympathy. It is sad to see many of those little Canadian companies suffer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: What will you do about it?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: I have had several meetings and discussions with these people. Their attitude is more responsible and rational than that of the Conservatives on the other side of the House. In all the meetings these people said that both orders of government must settle this, that both orders of government must move, and that there must be some compromise. They recognize that since the National Energy Program was announced, we have made some moves, some adjustments, and have shown some compromise.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: To take over the industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: To the contrary, and I will quote the hon. member for Assiniboia. In the parliamentary committee last night he said that the producing provinces have not budged an inch. We can check the blues; he had better not change them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: They should not budge an inch.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: This is what the hon. member for Assiniboia said.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Why should they?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: I presume he was speaking for the Tory Opposition when he spoke like this last night.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Why should they?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Now we hear from another member from Alberta, the respectable hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). He is asking "why should they?" That is the attitude of the Conservatives: sock it to the consumers, give more money to the industry, give the producing provinces whatever they want; they should not compromise.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: You give Mexico $50 and us $15.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: I am glad the ministers of energy for the producing provinces and the premiers, particularly the Premier of Alberta, have more judgment and are more reasonable than the hon. member for Bow River.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: That is why you have not reached an agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: They are ready and willing to make some concessions. I will meet with the minister of energy for Alberta on June 10; I am looking forward to that meeting. At our last meeting, we indicated that we were willing to be flexible and to compromise. There was such a recognition of this fact by the spokesmen for Alberta that they agreed to have another meeting to look at whatever flexibility they could introduce in their position. In that sense, they have shown a lot more judgment than the Conservative members from Alberta who are sitting in the House, particularly the hon. member for Bow River.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Try telling them why you pay Mexico $50 and us only $15.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Indeed we have indicated that there must be a settlement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: You will not answer that, will you?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: It is a matter of high priority. The Governor of the Bank of Canada said yesterday that it was a matter of the highest priority. We agree with that. On November 2, the Prime Minister stood in the House and said that Alberta does not like the program and that we were ready to sit down and talk about improvements and adjustments to it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: It took you about eight months to decide that.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: What happened between November 2 and early April? We have not been able to obtain a meeting with the government of Alberta. That is the situation; that has been the situation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Now you blame Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
There was a cutback of 60,000 barrels by the government of Alberta.
May 27, 1981

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: And it could be even more.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: The hon. member for Bow River is shouting that there will be another one on June 1. How will that help the negotiations? How will that help the average Canadian?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Buy it from Mexico at $50 a barrel.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: We know that it will not help the average Canadian, it will hurt him, because he will have to pay even more.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Buy it from Mexico at $50.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: We hear that the industry hurts. In its last report, the Alberta Energy Conservation Board said that at worst the National Energy Program in Alberta, perceived in its worst possible context, might reduce production by 50,000 to 60,000 barrels in Alberta by 1990. But that board, which is a board of the Alberta government, said that what was most damaging to the industry in Alberta at the present time was the cutbacks imposed by that government, and that those cutbacks this year would cut production by 180,000 barrels and would have an impact on the industry of over $200 million in Alberta. This is what is happening with the decisions of the government of Alberta, not the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Pay us a proper price then.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: The hon. member for Bow River says, "Pay us what you want."

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: No, pay us a proper price.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: That is the position of the Tories in this House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Fifty dollars for Mexico, $15 for Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: The Tories say that any provincial government may dictate to the national government what should be the national policy. We do not believe in that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Fifty dollars for Mexico, $15 for Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: We believe in compromise and good sense. We believe in national responsibility for all the people of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: We will fulfil our national responsibility.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Fifty dollars for Mexico, $15 for Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: We will negotiate and arrive at a deal which will be fair to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the minister must leave, but I hope that he will stay
National Energy Program
and hear me for a short while. When I listened to his speech he reminded me of a man whom Oscar Wilde described as someone who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Right on!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
It seems to me that once again the minister has thumped, pumped and spoken. It was not a speech he gave, it was more of a tirade, which indicates to me that the minister must be in trouble with his National Energy Program.
The message we received on this side of the House was the same old message: Ottawa knows best what is good for the west. Before the minister leaves I wish to quote-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: When will you say something of substance?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: If the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) would listen for a moment he will see that I will deal positively with how I think we can solve this problem with western Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext: Proceed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would remind the minister of a speech given in this House by the Right Hon. Lester Pearson on April 14, 1964, as reported in Hansard at page 2145. I see the minister is leaving, but he can read my remarks in Hansard tomorrow. At page 2145 of Hansard for April 14, 1964 Mr. Pearson was dealing with co-operative federalism. He said:
It is the task of Parliament, without regard to party; it is the challenge of statesmanship rising above faction, to find the solutions to our problems which are now more serious and more difficult than any we have faced in peacetime since 1867.
Mr. Pearson was dealing with the problems of Quebec in the 1960s. He was dealing with a quiet revolution in Quebec, which in a strange way has certain similarities to the kind of economic revolution which is happening in western Canada at the moment. As I understand it, that was the reason why members such as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) were elected to Parliament. Maybe the minister has forgotten some of the words of his mentor, the Right Hon. Mr. Pearson. The speech goes on:
We must find these solutions by agreement, not force them by compulsion. We cannot hope to find such agreement in our country if we cannot find a basis for it in our Parliament.
And what did we receive in this House today? A tirade mainly against the Conservative opposition, and secondly, against the provinces with regard to the whole energy problem.
The minister has left the chamber, but I offer three quite obvious points to him to which I hope his parliamentary secretary will reply. One, we do not have a pricing agreement with Alberta, and on June 1 Alberta will turn down the tap further and Canadian consumers will have to pay more for gasoline. It will be another "Lalonde levy", as we call it here. The Liberals call it a "Lougheed levy". The Albertans call it a "Lalonde" levy and I call it a "Lougheed-Lalonde levy". In any case, it will be an additional tax to pay for imported oil.

May 27, 1981
National Energy Program
That is a ridiculous situation, Mr. Speaker. The minister cannot just get up in the House and blame it on hon. members to my right, or on the provinces, although in a great many ways it is a shared blame. The minister is part of those negotiations. He must be flexible in the agreement. Is the minister or the parliamentary secretary prepared to stand up in this House and say, "Mr. Speaker, all right, we will withdraw the 8 per cent wellhead tax. We will withdraw it, change it, and we will be flexible"? Saying that would go a long way toward reaching an agreement. But you can bet your bottom dollar and your bottom barrel of oil that neither one of them will stand up in the House and say that. The minister is one of the inflexible parties.
The second point I offer to the government speakers to reply to is simply this. We heard from the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) of a downturn in the west, in Alberta, in oil exploration. I have the same figures and I could quote them. All the figures are before us and they will appear in Hansard as cited by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre. The minister stood up and quoted figures from Oilweek, which I personally think are old figures. They are really last year's projections before the National Energy Program came into effect. Those figures will not be borne out. There will be a downturn in the Alberta oil and gas economy, also in the economies of Saskatchewan and British Columbia. I do not believe any of those figures. I do believe the guys who came into my office. They are working men, and they also went to the minister's office. I see a member to my right nodding, they also went to his office. I looked at them, and as a lawyer the minister knows that the best evidence is live evidence, what we lawyers call viva voce evidence. I could judge their credibility. It seemed to me they were credible. They were small time industry workers and they told me they were suffering. I believed them. They are suffering from the National Energy Program. For the minister to stand up and say that they are not suffering is simply hogwash. It goes against the best evidence there is-they were there and they were suffering.
The third point I offer to the government arising out of the minister's speech is the fact that the minister says we are developing Canada lands. He is asking us to look at all the exploration which is taking place, for example Dome Petroleum and others who, with all that public money, are exploring and developing Canada lands. "Canada lands" means the north and the offshore, it does not mean Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, where the minister cannot be the dictator. I ask this question of the government for reply in this debate: why develop Canada lands when you have Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia to develop? That does not make any sense to me. Why go to the high costs in the Arctic and offshore when you have Alberta with conventional gas? This does not make any sense to me. I submit that it does not make any sense to the average Canadian either. As the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) was saying, and I do not agree with his philosophy, why buy imported offshore oil when we have Alberta oil? It does not make sense for the minister to say, "Let us develop Canada lands", except if we
accepted a rather Machiavellian interpretation of what the minister is doing. Is he saying that he will go around Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia rather than deal with them? That is exactly the opposite of what Mr. Pearson said in the House in terms of co-operative federalism.
The minister said in the House, as well, that well before the end of the decade, by 1990, the people of Canada will own over 50 per cent of the industry. We support that. Who doesn't? Maybe a few hon. members to my right who have an ideological hang-up on public ownership do not agree, thereby going against the entire Canadian social history and the history of their own party. But other than those few members, we on this side of the House support that effort. In Sault Ste. Marie in 1974 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that we would own 50 per cent of the industry by 1980. Mr. Speaker, there is just no credibility there.
I would like to deal, in the time I have left, with what I consider are now the positions of the three political parties in Canada on energy. I hope that when I am outlining our position I can suggest some principles upon which we can settle by negotiation the dispute with Alberta. I agree with all speakers that this is the number one problem. It is one of the big problems in the Canadian economy today.
I should say right away that both the Conservative spokesman and myself do not think that the National Energy Program is working. It was supposed to help Canadian companies; but these little guys, these Canadian companies, are telling us they are going out of business. Something is wrong there; and I will tell you what is wrong. What is wrong is that the major foreign-owned companies are making their profits downstream. By that I mean in marketing, in pipelining and in selling gasoline at the pumps. The little Canadian companies make their money and do their work in exploration and development. So what does the government do? It puts an 8 per cent wellhead tax at the exploration and development stage. Whom does this hurt? The little guys? One does not hear the big companies squealing. One hears the little guys squealing. So what kind of a Canadianization policy is that? To me it does not make sense, and that is one of the reasons we are opposing the National Energy Program. They are scared. My colleague said they are scared of the big companies. I will come back to that in a moment.
With respect to the Conservative policies outlined by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre, it seems to me it is simply that the industry should be given a free hand. He said, and I quote, "The pricing schedule is not sufficient to bring about new investment". That is the industry line: "Give us more and more and more." That is the line my friends to the right are taking. They believe it. They are advancing it. However, it seems to me it will result in high profits to the industry. There have been record profits over the past few years. It will result in continued foreign ownership. We must tackle that problem. There is no way of getting around it. Either we tackle it or we do not tackle it, and that kind of "let the industry have a free
May 27, 1981

hand" will mean continued foreign ownership. Finally, with continued foreign ownership, it will always mean pressure for high prices.
What is the Liberal policy? We have had a lot of fancy talk. In 1973 we had a national energy program. The Prime Minister said:
Its prime objective, to be reached before the end of the decade is self-sufficiency in oil and oil products.
In 1973, the big target was 1980. Now, in 1980, the target is 1990. The fact is that the government has not done anything very much in the past to really tackle the oil industry. What is it doing now? The minister says it plans to support renewables and conservation, but it gives $20 million to Canartech and $40 million to Imperial Oil to continue on with its development in the tar sands. Mr. Bertrand came out with a report in which he said the oil companies made excessive profits over the time the government was in office, and the time that the Conservatives were in office as well, and that these excessive profits and rip-offs were continuing. What did the government do? Well, Mr. Bertrand was moved; he went to the Antidumping Tribunal. He was dumped on the Anti-dumping Tribunal, and that is what happened.
The minister also talks about opening up the north. As we found out, the National Energy Program, in the opening up of the Canada lands in Bill C-48, has, in fact, brought problems to the north. The northern governments are upset and the native people are losing their rights. Because it cannot solve its dispute with Alberta, this government is prepared to bring in a national energy policy which will destroy the lands, in my submission, destroy the environment of Canada's north and destroy the native people in Canada. That is the bottom line.

We believe in Canadianization; but to us Canadi-anization does not mean to take over Petrofina, number eighteen from the list of companies. We would make Petro-Canada number one in the oil industry by taking over Imperial Oil. Second, we believe in conservation and renewables. We will put a massive effort into conservation and into renewables, not this picky little effort of the government, and we would follow some of the recommendations of the recent report of the task force of the House of Commons.
Third, we believe in provincial ownership. This is essential. I heard the hon. members applaud when the minister gave his last statement. I asked the hon. members on the opposite side, on the Liberal benches, to think about what the minister said. The fact is that the resources belong to the provinces, and that
National Energy Program
is in the Constitution. It is in the British North America Act. It is in the new Constitution, and that is generally accepted.
The provinces have been painted as the bad guys here. They have said that in spite of the fact that the resources belong to them, they are prepared to share. They are prepared not to ask for world price, but only for 75 per cent of the world price. They are even prepared to share the revenue they then get, recognizing that oil prices are extraordinary. We in the New Democratic Party reject world price. We do not believe in the world price; but we are prepared to listen to the provinces when they request their share and the prices they want.
For the federal government's share, if the federal government wants to subsidize oil prices in this company, then the federal government must take less of the amount. In a way, that respects the principle of provincial ownership, and it respects the problem we have in this country of not rushing the high oil prices right away. So in this country we can, in fact, have lower oil prices, but we can meet the requirements of the provincial governments. We can take off the 8 per cent wellhead tax and we can take off the 30-cent per thousand cubic feet gas tax because they are discriminatory taxes. They fall against the west.

If they continue to treat the west the way they are, they will have a separated west, or they will have-

speechtext:
I asked the hon. member to listen to what 1 am saying. I am saying that we must try to meet the legitimate requests. The hon. member is a Quebecer, and I suspect that he understands the legitimate request of the province to control its own resources, to get a fair price for them, and to not be pressed or told what to do by the federal government and to not be discriminated against, but to work with the federal government. The government does not go around putting a tax on electricity going to the United States. That is what I am trying to say. Outside the House, or maybe later if I have time, I will talk to the hon. member about that.
I want to conclude by saying that it is no good to have a national energy policy without having an increased public sector role. That is really the kind of modern world we are talking about. If we are going to have Canadianization, we must talk about that. We must also talk a little bit about not giving away all this kind of money which we propose to give away in the north as direct grants without getting some equity for the Canadian people and without getting some control.
Finally, we must tie into a national industrial strategy. The people are groping with that in this House. The Conservatives have suggested that there will be an impact in Ontario if we slow down oil production. We must flush that out and bring in shipbuilding in British Columbia where I come from. We are interested in that development as well. So we must tie into an industrial strategy.
Let me just conclude by saying we do not think the National Energy Program is working. We applaud all these great statements of Canadianization, conservation, substitution and so on. We want to see it work in practice. Too many Liberal statements in the past have turned out to be just pious hopes. I have suggested today, in I hope, a very positive, Pearsonian spirit, that we can reach an agreement with the provinces based on the principles I have set out. I hope to speak further on these principles in the House at another time. I think we can get this agreement very soon. The world will pass us by if we do not get together to solve the energy problem in this country. We will all suffer as a result.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak in this House on this very important subject. I am sorry that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is not present because I should like to bring a very positive direction to the energy question, particularly from those in the field and the people in the service and supply industry in my area who are suffering as a result of the energy dispute.
The minister referred to the import compensation program which he defended vigorously in the House just a few minutes ago. I should like to deal with the facts as they are in the field, with the international situation and also with the deficit that this country faces because of the import policies and compensation program of this government.
We import 150,000 barrels of oil per day from Mexico and Saudi Arabia which costs taxpayers $8.8 million per day. This is the equivalent of $1 million per hour for an eight-hour working day, to say nothing of the spin-off benefits that would accrue to the economy of the country if the minister would address the National Energy Program in a positive manner.
The National Energy Program should be the number one plank for solving the economic problems facing us today. Instead, it has become the number one business mistake made by any government in this century, particularly the government of which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is a member.
I want to deal with the local conditions in the province of Saskatchewan which the minister addressed, Mr. Speaker. He said that royalties in Saskatchewan are high. They are. The minister did not explain to the people of Canada, and particularly the people of eastern Canada who are not aware of the situation, that Saskatchewan wells have low production. The average production of a Saskatchewan oil well is 19 barrels; the average production in Alberta is 60 barrels. The minister is unfair to the people of Canada when he neglects to clarify that point.
I want to bring to the attention of the members of the House and all those who are interested in the national energy policy a situation which arose this past week in my riding of Assiniboia. There are 480 wells of which PanCanadian is the unit operator, covering 65 other oil companies. Production at those 480 wells has been cut by 75 per cent because in the production of 14,000 barrels per day throughout the last year, the companies lost $564,000. The energy picture in western Canada has been clouded since October 28, at a time when it should be having the biggest boom in its history. If this is not a serious situation, then I do not know what is.
In the Williston Basin, which is 100 miles south, in the area of Estevan, Weyburn, Radville and Midale, and the oil field of southern Saskatchewan which is a part of the Williston Basin, production has decreased by 75 per cent but the production in Williston-North Dakota has increased by 75 per cent. Mr. Speaker, 139 oil rigs have left. I recall that I was one of the first members to rise in this House and ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources if he did not fear that the oil rigs would be driven out of the country. He would not even admit to the possibility. That went on until last July and then began again last fall. We on this side of the House kept asking the minister whether he did not fear that his energy policy would drive the rigs out and he continued to defend his position, claiming that his policies would not have this effect. But, Mr. Speaker, we have lost 139 rigs.
As a result of Bill C-42, in 1972 we lost 65 oil rigs, not one of which has returned. Canada has one of the finest oil drilling fleets in the world, and it is being driven into the arms of Americans for their benefit instead of being used for the benefit of the Canadian people. All that drilling technology and so on is lost as well.
I should like now to turn to the service and supply industry. My colleague in the NDP mentioned that these people are
May 27, 1981

suffering very badly, and that is true. The industry is suffering as never before. There is about a 40 per cent reduction in employment, and small Canadian companies are being hurt.
The national energy policy pretends to address the Canadian situation and Canadianization of the industry, but in fact it is North Dakota, Montana and Texas which are being Canadi-anized. The rigs, the expertise and the investment capital are being driven out. All this will have far-reaching effects on our economy which will not soon be forgotten.
I should now like to turn to the matter of capital. For the past year I have been a member of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works which deals with energy. One member of the committee invariably asks how much capital is being spent in Canada. In most cases, whether the company concerned was Canadian or foreign, it was a fortunate thing for the Canadian people if they responded that as much as 25 per cent or 30 per cent of their total capital investment is spent in Canada.
The outflow of capital due to the government's energy policy and the minister's direction, is a frightening thing at this time, not only on the provincial scene but in the Canada lands as well. The Canadian people should not forget about this question because it is a very serious one in terms of the outflow of capital. There was mention of $1.5 billion to be spent by 1983 in the Canada lands. In testimony at the committee, the Norwegians made it abundantly clear that it is important to have the participation of all the majors in a project as large as Hibernia and the North Sea development.
It is most important that our energy policy address itself to that. I would like to get back to the local scene in Saskatchewan and elsewhere in western Canada and to what is happening there. There is a job loss of about 40 per cent. Many small operators possibly will not be able to hang on beyond another month or two as a result of this energy policy.
About 120 service and supply people from Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia appeared in Ottawa and painted a very serious and sad picture of the energy policy in Canada at this time. One hundred and thirty-nine rigs have left, as well as a great number of service rigs. There is 40 per cent unemployment and a 50 per cent cutback in exploration. The minister just said in this House that exploration would be up. It was intended that some 1,500 new wells would be drilled for exploration this year. It is now predicted that less than 700 new wells will be drilled. That is what is happening to our industry.
What about pricing? We now pay Mexico $42.50 a barrel for their oil. In Weyburn, Saskatchewan and in Alberta they pay $15.75 a barrel for heavier crude and $17.75 for lighter crude. This means a loss of jobs and a loss of opportunity for the people of this country. The minister of energy would prefer to buy oil from Mexico and Saudi Arabia at more than twice the price than give Canadians an opportunity to have jobs in their own country.
National Energy Program
What about the spin-off benefits for the people in Ontario, Quebec, those in the rubber industry and in manufacturing industries? I do not think there is one industry in Canada that would not be affected by the spin-off benefits from the production of oil in western Canada.
We have to be realistic. We in western Canada are good Canadians. We want to be a part of building this country. However, we want to be treated fairly. For 100 years the industrial sector of the world dominated the economic scene, not only in Toronto, Montreal, North America but across the world. Suddenly under OPEC, energy has become number one. Somehow western Canada is supposed to be second place to all of this activity and accept $15 a barrel while everyone else receives $40 a barrel. We are reasonable people. If the price of oil were increased by $4 a barrel, we would be receiving half the world price, which might be reasonable.
The members of this House and the people of Canada should start to think very seriously about what the minister of energy is doing to our country. As I said before, the people of western Canada are good Canadians. It just happens that we produce energy and food. I repeat, for 100 years the industrial sector of the world dominated the economic scene. Suddenly that sector is in trouble. The government which represents the golden horseshoe is saying to western Canadians that it will take with its big powerful hand of government what is necessary to keep this country going in the direction it has been. There is nothing wrong with that. We in western Canada think the federal government should have a fair share, but let us be reasonable. The future potential of Canada is great in manufacturing, energy and food, but we must work together as a country and a people.
When my colleague spoke previously, he warned about the dividing factor this energy policy has become under the direction of the minister of energy. It is very serious, and the frustration in western Canada is great. The minister must address the cold war between east and west as it relates to the energy policy.
I want to address another area of the energy policy. There is a very definite parallel in the direction in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is trying to lead this country with the Constitution and the energy policy. Make no mistake about it. I want to read a paragraph from the book "Reaction: The National Energy Program" put out by the Fraser Institute in Vancouver, British Columbia. I quote:
It is ironic that a program of government, designed to "secure the nation's energy future" should have such a damaging effect on the industrial sectors and the provinces uniquely capable of achieving it. Perhaps it is this inconsistency that has led some observers to claim that the new energy program is, in fact, a political document more concerned about short-run political objectives than energy security.
The direction of this government's energy policy is to nationalize the oil industry. Through Bill C-48, the move in the Canada lands and the 200-mile offshore in Canada lands, the federal government gives to the Crown corporation Petro-Can 25 per cent. There is a move to nationalize the oil industry. Through Bill C-48, it gives extraordinary powers and

May 27, 1981
National Energy Program
privileges to the minister of energy to take up as much as 50 per cent in some cases.
Because of my statement about the energy policy and the Constitution running parallel, I want to read something written by the Prime Minister on an earlier day when he wrote about the practice and theory of federalism dealing with constitutional reform and what he thought should happen to Canada in 1960, some 20 years ago. He wrote:
If the whole of the Canadian electorate could miraculously be converted to socialist ideals at one fell swoop, there would be no reason to discuss strategy in the present context. Socialism would be achieved with or without federalism, and socialist administrations would be installed at every level of governmental affairs, no matter the form of the Constitution.
I want to suggest to you that it is not by chance that running parallel with the nationalization direction and the Constitution of Canada is the energy policy. We are faced with a new direction that will lay an industry in western Canada flat on its back, if needs be, to achieve this end. That is exactly what is happening. The Canadianization program and the energy program of Canada at this time are taking that kind of direction.
What is the cost of the energy program to the people of Canada at this time? Some experts have projected that the cost of the energy program, including the cost of the spin-off effects amount to $1 million an hour, not taking into account the $8 million it is costing us to pay for the 150,000 barrels of oil we are bringing into Canada daily. 1 refer to the spin-off effects, the loss of jobs to Canadians, the loss to the car industry of Ontario and the loss to the manufacturing sector of Ontario.

speechtext:
I find in listening to the debate this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, that there seems to be some confusion on the part of the hon. member opposite who moved the motion. His motion reads:
That this House condemns the government's National Energy Program-
Yet the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) the same member who moved the motion condemning the National Energy Program, stated on January 22:
-I am in agreement with the broad objectives of the program. Who in this country would not be in favour of self-sufficiency, an increase in Canadian ownership, and fairness in pricing and revenue sharing?
On the one hand the hon. member opposite condemns the program, and on the other hand he says he is in agreement with it.
I suppose one should not be too surprised by that contradiction because one has aften heard of similar instances during the course of our energy debates in this House. We have, for example, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) going to Alberta, urging the Alberta government to "hang tough" as I believe he put it, in discussions with the national government, in demanding higher and higher oil prices. Yet
that same member when he returns to his native province of Newfoundland, or indeed here in the House of Commons, deplores the impact of higher oil prices on our economy and particularly on inflation. I do not know how the hon. member is able to reconcile those two obviously contradictory points of view.
Of course, we know of the confused Conservative Party attitude toward Petro-Canada. We have seen a series of positions taken, starting with outright condemnation, to gradual acceptance, and then to full acceptance. The other day the Leader of the Conservative Party (Mr. Clark) said, yes, after all, let us have Petro-Canada. That did not deter the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) who within a few days said, as reported in The Calgary Herald, that there are too many Crown corporations in Canada, let us get rid of some. Obviously, he added, Petro-Canada would be a good place to start. I do not think we need to feel any real surprise about the contradictions that are before us in this motion when we have, as I pointed out, the same hon. member supporting the National Energy Program and then turning around and condemning it.
In supporting the program, he specified three principal objectives: self-sufficiency in oil, added to the self-sufficiency in all other forms of energy which Canadians already enjoy; an increase in Canadian ownership; and fairness in pricing and revenue sharing. Let me deal with one or two of those points which, indeed, are principal objectives of the National Energy Program.
The petroleum industry is and will, of course, continue to be one of the largest and most prosperous sectors of our economy. The industry will benefit immensely from the effects of increased prices foreseen in the energy program, and particularly from the incentive grants to help ensure that Canadians achieve oil self-sufficiency, as well as benefiting from a greater degree of conservation and oil substitution.
We do not, however, accept that fundamental decisions affecting Canada's petroleum industry, that most dynamic sector of our economy, should be made primarily in the boardrooms of multinational companies outside Canada.
Since 1974, for example, the petroleum industry has been a major exporter of capital from Canada. Such capital exports would grow if we had not introduced the National Energy Program, and grow so substantially that our balance of payments situation would deteriorate causing yet further strain on the Canadian dollar and, indeed, fuelling inflation.
By ignoring the problem of foreign ownership and domination of the industry in the past, Canadians in fact forfeited a significant share of the benefits from the strong resource sector we fortunately have in this country. We have many sources of energy in rich supply, and we intend to ensure that our energy resources benefit all Canadians.
A recent report by the Royal Bank of Canada, noting the strong base for growth that we enjoy in this country, offered the following appraisal of the Canadian economy. It predicted that over this decade employment opportunities will increase
May 27, 1981

faster than the growth of the labour force. The Royal Bank estimated that the unemployment rate will fall to 6 per cent by 1985 and about 4 per cent by 1990, which is in fact, in the statistician's terms, almost no unemployment at all. The bank went on to suggest that Canada's potential growth rate will remain above that of the United States and rank second only to Japan among the seven major industrialized countries. I note these forecasts, Mr. Speaker, because that is the context in which the energy developments of the months and years ahead will bring benefit to all Canadians.
In the Atlantic provinces energy resources are behind much of the Atlantic renaissance, and that certainly will continue. Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Alberta will, of course, be the major beneficiaries of future energy developments in the area of conventional oil and in oil sands. It is against that background that we are working toward an agreement with the government of Alberta. I am sure that all members of the House look toward that agreement emerging in the time ahead.
[DOT] <1750)
Throughout the industrialized world, oil-fuelled inflation remains a persistent problem. We have noted how the two major OPEC-imposed price increases of 1973 and 1979 led to a rapid growth in inflation throughout the industrialized world. Yet we here in Canada have the opportunity to reduce that impact and to cushion the blow on our economy by developing our own resources.
Unlike hon. members opposite, we on this side of the House favour a made-in-Canada oil policy, not one that is made by OPEC, so as to benefit all Canadian consumers. Apart from sheltering consumers from the severe impact of unpredictable oil price hikes imposed from outside our country, we shall encourage all Canadian explorers and producers of oil and gas in Canada to participate to a yet greater degree in the industry. We shall do that through Canadianization and, through the activities of Petro-Canada.
I want to cite a few examples of the growing success of our Canadianization program. Obviously Canadian companies see the petroleum incentives program announced in the National Energy Program as a catalyst for putting together deals with largely foreign companies which control so much of the land both in the frontier areas and in the provinces. There is growing evidence too-we have seen articles and news announcements in profusion recently-about the reaction to the incentives which are being offered. There are high expectations for the east coast. Not only will the major Hibernia and Sable Island deposits bring great benefit, but other opportunities are also being identified, partly in response to the initiatives taken under the National Energy Program.
In the Arctic the recent discovery of oil by the Panarctic consortium is encouraging. In the Beaufort Sea, Dome's activities are clearly accelerating, and development will reach record levels. Other Canadian companies such as Norcen are joining with foreign-controlled corporations in the search in the Arctic areas as well.
National Energy Program
Therefore, there is certainly no need to be sombre. Indeed, there is every reason to be expectant and optimistic about the opportunities on Canada lands, the frontier areas of Canada. As the minister noted, oil exploration activity on Canada lands this year is at record levels. It shows every prospect of continuing and reaching much higher levels in the years ahead. That is an ample refutation of claims by hon. members opposite who continue to argue against the thrust of the National Energy Program.
I have cited several major activities on Canada lands, but I would not want to pass over the fact that other corporations have recently announced new initiatives. Husky Oil has indicated an intention to play a new role in offshores exploration. Real-West Energy Corporation has acquired potentially the largest single shareholdings in Asamera Inc. and United Canso, a step in the direction of Canadianization and further development. There is growing evidence that many foreign-owned companies are adjusting their ownership structures to take advantage of the incentives offered under the National Energy Program. The government's agreement with Dome Petroleum regarding the creation of Dome Canada is only the first example of many which I am sure will emerge in the time ahead.
I could cite, for example, the case of PanCanadian Petroleum which has formed a new east coast exploration group with Norcen and Roxy Petroleum. Another Calgary company, Ranchmen's Resources, has restructured its shares using the Dome Canada arrangement as a model.
I cite these examples to indicate to hon. members opposite that the National Energy Program constitutes a new and innovative approach to energy policy in Canada. For aggressive and forward-looking companies the program obviously offers immense benefits. Contrary to what the previous speaker said about his fears of some obscure move toward nationalization, we see in fact ample evidence of private entrepreneurs in Canada taking the initiative to ensure that the Canadianization goals set by the government will be achieved.
Of course, not all Canadians can hope to participate in the Canadianization of the industry through the acquisition of shares. For those who cannot take or do not take that route, participation is achieved through Petro-Canada. Canadians can all benefit through their own Crown corporation in major oil and gas activities. I find it ironic that we still hear from hon. members opposite attacks on Petro-Canada. Any brief review of the past years will indicate a remarkable confusion on the part of hon. members opposite about where they stand on the question of a national petroleum corporation.
I remind hon. members that in 1974 when we created Petro-Canada it was to provide a window on the industry. It was to provide a toe-hold, so to speak, at the exploration and research end of the petroleum industry, with an initial capital investment of some $500 million. I remind hon. members that at that time the Leader of the Opposition said that Petro-Canada would become a $500 million white elephant.
Through the 1979 election campaign confusion and contradiction in the Conservative ranks increased even further. The

May 27, 1981
National Energy Program
free enterprise hawks were whetting their appetites at the thought of the carrion which was about to be created from the national oil company. Yet that was the same year, 1979, in which the president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce said of Petro-Canada said: "It is serving a purpose, and my own feeling is that it should be left alone". Indeed, in a very short time we noted the chairman of Imperial Oil and other leaders in the petroleum industry recognizing that there was an important role for Petro-Canada to play. Perhaps as a result of those or other factors, the Conservative party then changed course from its days in opposition, and when it came to power it passed through a remarkable series of acrobatics about who should own Petro-Canada, what its share structure should be, whether it should be a Crown corporation or not,
whether it should be partly owned by the public or through direct share ownership, whether it should be entirely in private hands, and so forth.
